questions.stem: A pharmacist has to state how much glucose a patient receives in a fixed volume of medicine, so she measures the volume of the liquid instead of weighing it. Name the method of expressing concentration she should use and state how many grams of glucose 100 millilitres of a 5% glucose solution contains.

questions.stem:
In a science period, Ravi stirred one spatula of common salt into 50 mL of water in a 100 mL beaker, Neha stirred one spatula of chalk powder into 50 mL of water, and Imran added a few drops of milk to 50 mL of water and stirred. Their teacher passed laser light through each beaker and asked the class to view it from the side, in a direction perpendicular to the beam, warning them never to look straight into it. They then filtered each mixture. Two beakers, one of sugar in water and one of sand in water, stood on the desk, and the teacher asked why these two do not belong to one group.

State the direction from which the class must view the laser beam and the safety precaution the teacher insists on. (ii) Name the type of mixture in the beaker of sugar in water, giving its other name, and name the type of mixture in the beaker of sand and water. (iii) Ravi says that since both beakers hold a solid mixed with water, one name should serve for both. Using what the class can observe in the two beakers, explain why he is wrong.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (i) From the side of the beaker, perpendicular to the beam; never look directly into it, as it can cause irreversible eye damage. (ii) Sugar in water: a homogeneous mixture, also called a solution. Sand in water: a heterogeneous mixture. (iii) The sugar mixture stays uniform, equally sweet in the first sip and the last, while the sand particles are visible and settle with time.

questions.subject: Science
questions.stem:
At a school exhibition, a Class 9 student named Diya stood beside a table of glass beakers. One beaker held vinegar, which she said was acetic acid in water. A second held soda, an aerated drink with carbon dioxide dissolved in water. A third held sand stirred into water, and Diya pointed out that the grains could easily be seen and that they settled with time. A visitor asked about sugar, and Diya answered that a well-stirred mixture of sugar and water is just as sweet in the first sip as in the last, and that it keeps a uniform composition throughout. The visitor then asked whether the sand beaker could be given the same name as the sugar beaker.

State the type of mixture in the vinegar beaker, in the soda beaker and in the beaker of stirred sand and water. (ii) Name the type of mixture in the sugar beaker and give its other name. (iii) Diya says the sand beaker cannot be given the same name as the sugar beaker. Using the observations she describes, explain why the two cannot share one name.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (i) Vinegar and soda are homogeneous mixtures; the stirred sand and water is a heterogeneous mixture. (ii) A homogeneous mixture, also called a solution. (iii) The sugar mixture keeps a uniform composition throughout, while in the sand and water mixture the grains are visible and settle with time, so it is not uniform.

questions.subject: Science
questions.stem:
Three groups prepared mixtures in a science period. Group A added one spatula of common salt to 50 mL of water. Group B added one spatula of chalk powder to 50 mL of water, and Group C added a few drops of milk to 50 mL of water. Each group looked at its beaker and recorded whether the particles were visible. Each group then set up a filtration apparatus and filtered its mixture separately, noting any residue left on the filter paper. The teacher asked them to predict what they would see if the beakers stood undisturbed for a few minutes. At the end they agreed the mixtures were not all of one type.

State what each group recorded after looking at its beaker and what it noted after filtering its mixture. (ii) Name the two types into which mixtures are classified. (iii) The three groups agreed that the mixtures they prepared were not all of one type. Using the observations that decide this, explain how a mixture whose particles are visible and settle with time differs from one whose composition is uniform throughout.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (i) Whether the particles were visible, and whether any residue was left on the filter paper. (ii) Homogeneous mixtures and heterogeneous mixtures. (iii) A mixture whose particles are visible and settle with time is not uniform, so it is heterogeneous; one with a uniform composition throughout is homogeneous.

questions.subject: Science
questions.stem:
Rhea works in the dispensary of a small clinic. Instead of weighing every solid she mixes, she measures the volume of the liquid, because that is easier for her. A doctor asks her what a bottle labelled 5% glucose solution contains, and she explains that the percentage tells how many grams of the solute are present in 100 millilitres of the solution. Rhea also has to make a pesticide spray for a rice crop: she mixes 1 mL of liquid pesticide with sufficient water to form 100 mL of spray solution. Her friend asks her about the saline drip used in hospitals, which is 0.9 % m/v sodium chloride, or common salt, in water.

Name the method of expressing concentration that suits Rhea's situation of measuring the volume of a liquid instead of weighing it, and give the two symbols by which it is written. (ii) State what the label on the 5% glucose solution bottle tells the doctor about the amount of glucose. (iii) Rhea's friend points out that the perfumes and cosmetics in the shop next door are liquids too, and asks why they are not labelled in the same way as the glucose solution. Using the situations in which the methods are used, explain.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (i) Mass by volume percentage (% m/v or % w/v). (ii) It shows how many grams of the solute are present in 100 millilitres of the solution. (iii) Perfumes, cosmetics and vinegar are made by mixing two miscible liquids, which is the case volume by volume percentage is meant for; a glucose solution in a clinic is a case where measuring the volume of the liquid is easier than weighing it.

evidence:
B. Mass by volume percentage (% m/v or % w/v)
This method is used where measuring the volume of a liquid is easier
than weighing it, for example, in medicines and laboratories.

example is 5% glucose solution (Fig. 5.4b). It tells us how many grams of the
solute is present in 100 millilitres of the solution.
